title: The history of the harmonium
tagline: More than 3,000 years from a Chinese mouth organ with tiny bamboo reeds, through the parlours and churches of Europe, to the hand-pumped box that sings with India's temples, gurdwaras, qawwalis and film songs.
intro: A harmonium makes sound with free reeds: thin metal tongues that swing back and forth through a slot when air pushes past them. The idea began in China and Southeast Asia, reached Europe in the 1700s, and became a keyboard instrument with bellows in France. Then Indian makers shrank it, put the bellows on the back, and made it an instrument you play sitting on the floor, where it became so loved that some people tried to ban it.

eras.name: Reeds you blow
eras.summary: In China and Southeast Asia people play mouth organs like the sheng and the khaen, where breath makes little free reeds sing inside bamboo pipes.

eras.name: Europe's reed organs
eras.summary: European inventors put free reeds inside boxes with keyboards and bellows. The French pressure harmonium and the American suction organ fill churches and homes, and scientists use harmoniums to study tuning.

eras.name: Made in India
eras.summary: The harmonium arrives with missionaries and traders. A Calcutta maker turns it into a small, hand-pumped box for floor playing, and it spreads to theatre, temples, gurdwaras and music schools.

eras.name: Banned and beloved
eras.summary: Critics say its fixed notes do not suit Indian music. All India Radio bans it for about 30 years, while musicians go on playing it everywhere else.

eras.name: A voice of its own
eras.summary: The ban eases, qawwali carries the harmonium around the world, Indian masters win national honours for it, and inventors build harmoniums that can play India's finer notes.

events.title: The sheng: the first free reeds
events.text: Mouth organs called sheng and yu are mentioned on oracle bones from about 3,000 years ago. A sheng has bamboo pipes standing in a wind chest, and each pipe hides a tiny reed that swings freely through a slot. Cousins such as the khaen of Laos use the same trick.
events.why: Every harmonium, accordion and harmonica still uses this free reed idea.

events.title: Mouth organs buried with a marquis
events.text: When the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng was dug up in 1978, it held a whole orchestra, including six sheng made from gourds and pipes. Water had filled the tomb and kept the instruments safe for about 2,400 years. Their reeds were made of bamboo.
events.why: They are some of the oldest free-reed instruments that survive.

events.title: A machine that says its vowels
events.text: The Imperial Academy of Sciences in St Petersburg offered a prize for explaining how we make vowel sounds. Kratzenstein won in 1780 with pipes shaped like mouths, each sounded by a free reed, that could say A, E, I, O and U. It is one of the first talking machines.
events.why: It showed Europe how useful the free reed could be.

events.title: Free reeds join the church organ
events.who: Abbé Georg Joseph Vogler, inspired by organ builder Kirsnik
events.text: In 1788 the travelling musician Abbé Vogler met Kirsnik, an organ builder who put free reeds in organ pipes, in St Petersburg. From 1790 Vogler added free-reed stops to about 30 organs around Europe. He also built his own touring organ, the orchestrion.
events.why: It carried the free reed from a curiosity into real instruments.

events.title: An organ that can get louder and softer
events.text: Grenié built the orgue expressif, a small organ with free reeds. He showed it in 1810, though the 1911 Britannica says his first one was finished in 1812. When the player pushed more air, the reeds sounded louder, which a normal organ pipe cannot do without going out of tune.
events.why: Control over the air pressure became the harmonium's special power.

events.title: The harmonium gets its name
events.text: Debain patented a keyboard instrument with free reeds and foot-pumped bellows and called it the harmonium. He put several sets of reeds with different tone colours on one keyboard, chosen with stops. The 1911 Britannica and most sources give 1840 for the patent, though a few say 1842.
events.why: Almost every reed organ made afterwards follows his basic plan.

events.title: America sucks instead of blows
events.text: Carhart patented a bellows that pulls air in through the reeds instead of pushing it out through them. Melodeons with suction bellows soon spread through American homes. After 1885 Mason & Hamlin also adopted suction, and it became the American standard, while the French harmonium kept pushing air.
events.why: It split reed organs into two families: pressure harmoniums and suction organs.

events.title: Double expression
events.text: Mustel, a carpenter from Le Havre, patented his double expression in 1854. Knee levers let the player make the bass and the treble louder or softer on their own. His harmonium won a first-class medal at the Paris Exposition of 1855, and Mustel harmoniums became among the most admired in Europe.
events.why: It let players shape the sound almost like a singer.

events.title: A reed organ in every parlour
events.who: Mason & Hamlin, Estey and many other firms
events.where: Boston, Massachusetts, and Brattleboro, Vermont, USA
events.text: Mason & Hamlin, founded in Boston in 1854, launched its American organ in 1861 and showed it in Paris in 1867. Between the 1850s and 1920s, several million reed organs and melodeons were made in the United States and Canada. Estey alone made about half a million.
events.why: The reed organ became the ordinary family's keyboard, long before pianos were cheap.

events.title: Scientists tune harmoniums to pure intervals
events.text: In his 1863 book On the Sensations of Tone, Helmholtz used a harmonium with 24 notes to the octave, tuned so its chords were perfectly pure. In 1872 to 1873 Bosanquet had a harmonium built with 53 notes to the octave. Steady reeds made harmoniums perfect for hearing tiny differences in tuning.
events.why: It showed that the usual 12 equal notes are a compromise, the same worry later raised in India.

events.title: A famous piece for harmonium
events.text: Dvořák wrote his Bagatelles for two violins, cello and harmonium. His friend's flat had no piano, only a harmonium, so he wrote for that. It was first played there in February 1879.
events.why: It shows how common the harmonium was in European homes.

events.title: The West moves on
events.text: Electronic organs appeared in the 1930s, and reed organs started to fade in Europe and America. Estey, the last big North American maker, stopped making reed organs in the mid-1950s. By then India had become the harmonium's real home.
events.why: The instrument almost vanished in the West just as it thrived in South Asia.

events.title: The harmonium reaches India
events.who: Missionaries, traders and the Tagore family
events.text: Portable reed organs came to India in the mid-1800s, carried by missionaries, chaplains and traders to accompany hymns. In 1860 Dwijendranath Tagore used an imported one in his private theatre in Calcutta. Nobody knows exactly where in India the first one arrived.
events.why: It planted a European church instrument in a land with a very different music.

events.title: A harmonium handbook in Bengal
events.text: S. M. Tagore, a music scholar who ran a music school, published Harmonium Sutra, a guide to playing the harmonium with an Indian notation. Early music schools across North India taught the harmonium to large numbers of students.
events.why: Students wanted harmoniums, which gave makers a reason to build one for Indian music.

events.title: The hand-pumped harmonium
events.text: Dwarkanath Ghose started a music business in Calcutta in 1875, the firm later called Dwarkin. He is widely credited with the Indian harmonium: a small box you pump by hand from the back, played sitting on the floor with singers and drummers. He made it simpler and tougher, and added drone stops for Indian music.
events.why: This is the design almost every Indian harmonium still follows.

events.title: Theatre carries it south
events.who: A Parsi theatre troupe; the twin brothers Nanji and Mahanji
events.text: Parsi theatre companies used the harmonium to accompany songs on stage all over India. For the coronation of Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV in 1902, a troupe brought harmoniums to Mysore. Two harmonium players kept by the king were among the first to teach it in Carnatic music.
events.why: Travelling theatre spread the harmonium faster than any school could.

events.title: Kirtan at the Golden Temple
events.text: The harmonium is thought to have entered kirtan at the Golden Temple in the early 1900s, probably between 1905 and 1908. Over the next century it replaced most of the older string instruments in Sikh devotional singing. Today ragi groups sing there for about 20 hours a day.
events.why: It became the sound of Sikh worship for millions of people.

events.title: The harmonium in Marathi musical theatre
events.text: Govindrao Tembe, a largely self-taught harmonium player, composed the music for the play Manapman in 1910. Natya sangeet, the song-filled Marathi stage, used the harmonium as its main instrument, following pioneers like Bhaiyya Ganpatrao. Tembe later wrote music for the first Marathi talkie film in 1932.
events.why: Theatre and then film songs made the harmonium part of everyday Indian music.

events.title: A harmonium for the 22 shrutis
events.who: Ernest Clements and Krishnaji Ballal Deval
events.text: Deval measured the notes of the singer Abdul Karim Khan and argued they matched the ancient Indian idea of 22 shrutis, or microtones. With Ernest Clements he designed a shruti harmonium tuned to pure ratios, which was patented in London in 1911. It was shown at the All India Music Conference in Baroda in 1916 but did not catch on.
events.why: It was the first attempt to make the harmonium fit Indian tuning instead of banning it.

events.title: The bane of Indian music
events.text: Tagore had played the harmonium in his youth, as his own memoirs describe. Later he wrote the famous line calling it that bane of Indian music, and said he practised with a tanpura so as not to be a slave to the keyboard. The harmonium was kept out of his school at Santiniketan for a long time.
events.why: His words made the harmonium a symbol in the fight over what Indian music should sound like.

events.title: A British scholar calls it a menace
events.text: In his book The Music of Hindostan, Fox Strangways called the harmonium a serious menace to Indian music. He said it was out of tune with itself and would spoil singers' ears. He also noted it had already reached the remotest parts of India.
events.why: His book spread the idea that the harmonium's fixed notes did not belong in ragas.

events.title: All India Radio bans the harmonium
events.who: Lionel Fielden, Controller of Broadcasting, after a campaign by John Foulds
events.text: The composer John Foulds, who ran Western music at All India Radio, wrote in 1938 that the harmonium's tuning did not fit Indian music. Soon after, the radio banned it from its Indian music programmes, and the ban took effect on 1 March 1940. Protesting musicians staged a mock funeral and buried eleven harmoniums.
events.why: For three decades, India's national radio refused to play its most popular accompanying instrument.

events.title: The ban is partly lifted
events.who: All India Radio and the Sangeet Natak Akademi
events.text: After a 1970 meeting of music experts, All India Radio allowed top grade singers and qawwali groups to use the harmonium as an accompaniment. Solo harmonium recitals stayed off its main music programmes for many years after. One critic argued the harmonium should not be treated as an untouchable.
events.why: The harmonium was back on air, but still not trusted as a solo instrument.

events.title: The samvadini
events.text: Manohar Chimote worked for years to play full classical ragas as harmonium solos, with slow openings and fast strokes like a sitar. He retuned and revoiced his instrument and in 1972 gave it a new name: samvadini, the one that creates harmony.
events.why: It was a bold claim that the harmonium could be a classical solo voice.

events.title: Qawwali reaches Carnegie Hall
events.text: Ghulam Farid Sabri and Maqbool Ahmed Sabri from Karachi sang and played harmonium in their qawwali group. In 1975 they performed at Carnegie Hall in New York, said to be the first qawwali performance in the West. Their harmonium drones and rolling rhythms amazed new audiences.
events.why: It carried the harmonium's sound far beyond South Asia.

events.title: Nusrat's party wins over the world
events.who: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan and Farrukh Fateh Ali Khan
events.text: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan's qawwali group sang for hours at the WOMAD festival in 1985, and it launched his world career. His brother Farrukh played lead harmonium in the group for more than 25 years. Fans in England called him the King of the Harmonium.
events.why: Millions of people around the world first heard the Indian harmonium through qawwali.

events.title: National honours for harmonium players
events.who: Mehmood Dhaulpuri, Appa Jalgaonkar and Tulsidas Borkar
events.text: Mehmood Dhaulpuri accompanied great singers such as Bhimsen Joshi, Kishori Amonkar and Girija Devi. In 2006 he received the Padma Shri, and he is widely described as the first harmonium player to get it. Appa Jalgaonkar had won a Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in 2000, and Tulsidas Borkar received the Padma Shri in 2016.
events.why: India's government was now honouring the instrument its radio had once banned.

events.title: The 22-shruti harmonium
events.text: Doctor and musicologist Vidyadhar Oke built a harmonium with small knobs under the keys that let each note be nudged to the right shruti. Singer Rahul Deshpande used it on stage at the Sawai Gandharva festival in Pune, in December 2006 or 2007 depending on the source. Oke later received an Indian patent for it.
events.why: It tries to fix the very tuning problem that got the harmonium banned.

events.title: A call to bring back the strings
events.who: Akal Takht Jathedar Giani Harpreet Singh; the SGPC
events.text: The Akal Takht asked the SGPC, which runs the Golden Temple, to bring back traditional string instruments in kirtan within three years, calling the harmonium colonial. The SGPC said it would revive the strings step by step at the Golden Temple, but had no plans to throw out the harmonium. The debate about this imported instrument is still alive.
events.why: More than 140 years after Dwarkin, people still argue about whether the harmonium truly belongs.

facts: A harmonium reed never hits anything: the thin brass tongue swings through its slot, chopping the air into puffs.
The French harmonium pushes air through its reeds, while the American reed organ sucks air through them.
When All India Radio banned the harmonium in 1940, protesting musicians held a mock funeral and buried eleven harmoniums.
Estey, just one American maker, built about half a million reed organs between 1846 and 1955.
Rabindranath Tagore called the harmonium the bane of Indian music, yet his own memoirs describe him singing to one.
